facts.capital: Montpelier (the least populous state capital in the U.S.)
facts.statehood_note: Vermont was the first state to join the Union after the original 13. Before that it governed itself as the independent Vermont Republic from 1777 to 1791.

symbols.name: Charlotte the whale, a beluga skeleton (1993)

facts.name_origin: The name Vermont was adopted in 1777 for the Vermont Republic. It comes from French words meaning "Green Mountain(s)," after the mountain range that runs down the middle of the state.

government.chambers: Vermont Senate (30 members) and Vermont House of Representatives (150 members), 180 lawmakers in all. Every member serves a two-year term. It is a part-time legislature that usually meets from January to about mid-May.
government.executive: Governor (2-year term). Vermonters also elect a Lieutenant Governor, Secretary of State, State Treasurer, Auditor of Accounts, and Attorney General, each for two years.
government.courts: Vermont Supreme Court (5 justices who serve six-year terms) is the highest court. The Superior Court is the main trial court and the only court that holds jury trials.
government.local: 14 counties, which have very few powers of their own and mostly serve as court districts. Towns govern themselves through town meeting, where citizens vote directly. Vermont's four Abenaki tribes are state recognized.
government.constitution: Vermont's first constitution (1777) was the first state constitution to outlaw slavery, though it allowed some exceptions. The current constitution dates from 1793. On November 8, 2022, voters approved an amendment (88.7 percent yes) that bans slavery and indentured servitude in any form.
government.kid_line: "That all persons are born equally free and independent, and have certain natural, inherent, and unalienable rights ... Slavery and indentured servitude in any form are prohibited." (Vermont Constitution, Chapter I, Article 1, as amended in 2022)

long_ago.about: The first people arrived in Vermont soon after the glaciers melted, about 11,000 to 13,000 years ago. They lived in small groups of about thirty people who moved with the seasons to hunt and gather.

From about 9,500 to 3,000 years ago, small bands hunted, gathered, and fished from campsites along rivers and lakes. Around 6000 BC, people camped at the John's Bridge site in Swanton to hunt and fish.

The Western Abenaki, including the Sokoki, Cowasuck, and Missisquoi, call their homeland Ndakinna. About 10,000 Abenaki lived in Vermont before Europeans came; they lived in dome-shaped wigwams made of bark and saplings, traveled by canoe and snowshoe, and boiled maple sap into syrup, which they taught to colonists.
From about 1200 to 1600 CE, Abenaki women grew corn, beans, and squash in fertile river valleys. Villages along Connecticut River streams in southeastern Vermont could hold up to 1,000 people.
Mohican and Penacook people also lived in Vermont alongside the Abenaki before European settlement, and the Mohawk were active in the area when Europeans arrived.

first_peoples.today_note: Vermont has four state-recognized Abenaki tribes but no federally recognized tribes. Abenaki leaders say their people have lived here continuously for about 12,000 years, even though colonists, and as late as 2002 the state Attorney General's office, claimed they had left. Starting in the 1930s, Vermont's eugenics program targeted Abenaki families, and many hid their identity. Some Abenaki took refuge at Odanak (St. Francis) in Quebec starting in the 1670s, where an Abenaki First Nation still lives.
sites: Missisquoi River area, Swanton (Abenaki village site; John's Bridge site used about 6000 BC)
Lake Champlain and the Champlain Valley (Abenaki homeland, Ndakinna)
Connecticut River valley (Sokoki and Cowasuck Abenaki villages; dozens of ancient pottery sites)

history.event: After the glaciers melt, the first people arrive in Vermont. The land is still pressed down by the ice, and the Champlain Sea, an arm of the Atlantic Ocean, fills the Champlain Valley.
Abenaki women farm corn, beans, and squash in river valleys, and large Abenaki villages grow along the rivers.
Samuel de Champlain leads the first known European expedition to Lake Champlain.
The French build Fort Sainte Anne on Isle La Motte; it is abandoned by 1670. European diseases such as smallpox kill many Indigenous people.
Waranoki Chief Gray Lock builds a stone fort on the banks of the Missisquoi River.

Vermont declares itself an independent republic and writes the first state constitution to outlaw slavery for adults, though with exceptions. On August 16, militia defeat British troops sent to capture the supply depot at Bennington; the Battle of Bennington is fought just over the line, near Walloomsac, New York.
Vermont joins the United States as the 14th state, the first after the original 13.
In Windsor v. Jacob, the Vermont Supreme Court says "no inhabitant of the State can hold a slave." Even so, some Vermonters had bought enslaved people elsewhere and kept them as household servants.
Alexander Twilight graduates from Middlebury College, the first African American graduate of an American college.
Rokeby, a farm in Ferrisburgh that is now a museum, shelters two freedom seekers escaping slavery on the Underground Railroad.
Alexander Twilight is elected to the Vermont legislature, the first African American to serve in a U.S. state legislature.
Frederick Douglass gives a speech in Ferrisburgh, Vermont.
More than 33,000 Vermonters, including Black Vermonters, serve in the Union army during the Civil War.
In the St. Albans Raid, Confederate soldiers dressed as civilians rob banks in St. Albans, taking more than $200,000; it is the northernmost land action of the Civil War.

trailblazers.name: Gray Lock
trailblazers.text: Gray Lock was a Waranoki chief in the time of the colonial wars between Abenaki people and English colonists. In 1723 he built a stone fort on the banks of the Missisquoi River, near the Missisquoi Abenaki village.

trailblazers.name: Lucy Terry Prince
trailblazers.text: Lucy Terry was taken from West Africa as a small child and enslaved in Deerfield, Massachusetts, where in 1746 she composed "Bars Fight," the earliest known poem by an African American. After gaining her freedom, she and her husband, Abijah Prince, settled in Guilford, Vermont, in 1764, and she spoke up boldly for her family, including a three-hour appeal to Williams College trustees to admit her son.

trailblazers.name: Lemuel Haynes
trailblazers.text: Lemuel Haynes was the first Black person in America to serve as pastor of a white congregation. He led the West Parish church in Rutland for about 30 years, and in 1804 Middlebury College gave him an honorary degree, the first such degree given to an African American.

trailblazers.name: Alexander Twilight
trailblazers.group: Black American man, educator and lawmaker
trailblazers.text: Alexander Twilight, born in Corinth, Vermont, graduated from Middlebury College in 1823 as the first African American graduate of an American college. In 1836 he became the first African American elected to a U.S. state legislature, and as principal of the Orleans County Grammar School he built Athenian Hall in Brownington, the first granite public building in Vermont (now the Old Stone House Museum).

trailblazers.name: Clarina Howard Nichols
trailblazers.group: White woman, journalist and women's rights leader
trailblazers.text: Clarina Howard Nichols, born in West Townshend, Vermont, edited the Windham County Democrat newspaper and pushed for women's property rights. In 1852 she became the first woman to address the Vermont Legislature, asking that women be allowed to vote in school elections, a step toward equal voting rights.

trailblazers.name: Martin Henry Freeman
trailblazers.text: Martin Henry Freeman was born in Rutland, Vermont, and gave the salutatory address when he graduated from Middlebury College in 1849. He became president of the Allegheny Institute (later Avery College) in Pittsburgh, the first African American college president in the United States, and later led Liberia College in Monrovia, Liberia.

trailblazers.name: Mary Annette Anderson
trailblazers.text: Mary Annette Anderson was born in Shoreham, Vermont, the daughter of a formerly enslaved man who bought his own farm after the Civil War. In 1899 she was valedictorian at Middlebury College, its first woman of color graduate, and the first woman of color inducted into Phi Beta Kappa, a national honor society; she went on to teach at Howard University.

landforms: Green Mountains, running north to south through the middle of the state
Mount Mansfield, the highest point (about 4,400 feet)
Northeast Highlands, granite mountains in the northeast
Champlain Valley, with the state's best farmland
Vermont Valley, between the Green and Taconic mountains
waters: Lake Champlain, on the western border and the lowest point in the state (95 feet)
Winooski, Lamoille, Missisquoi, White, and Batten Kill rivers, and Otter Creek
geography.regions: Vermont is often divided into six regions: the Green Mountains, Northeast Highlands, Taconic Mountains, Vermont Valley, Champlain Valley, and Connecticut River Valley (Vermont Piedmont).

ecosystems.name: Northern forests
ecosystems.about: Forests cover much of Vermont, with hardwoods like birch, beech, and maple and softwoods like hemlock, spruce, and pine higher up. White-tailed deer, foxes, moose, beavers, and bobcats are common.

ecosystems.name: Lake Champlain and its rivers
ecosystems.about: Vermont's lakes support trout, salmon, bass, and pickerel; the brook trout and walleye are state fish. Archaic peoples fished along Vermont's rivers and lakes thousands of years ago.

ecosystems.name: Champlain Valley farmland
ecosystems.about: The Champlain Valley holds most of Vermont's best farmland. Dairy farming is a major part of Vermont agriculture, and the state has nearly half as many cows as people.

science.weather: Vermont has warm, humid summers and long, cold, snowy winters, with the heaviest snow in the mountains. Floods are the biggest hazard: the Great Vermont Flood of 1927 and Tropical Storm Irene in 2011 caused major damage, and the state is getting rainier overall.
science.resources: Vermont makes more maple syrup than any other state, about half of the nation's supply. Dairy farming (and cheddar cheese), forestry, granite and marble quarrying (especially around Barre and Rutland), and tourism, including ski resorts, are key to the economy.
science.highlight: Charlotte the whale: in 1849, railroad workers near Charlotte dug up the bones of a 12-foot beluga whale, far from any ocean. About 11,000 years ago, after the glaciers pressed the land down, the Champlain Sea filled the valley, and the whale died there. It became Vermont's state fossil in 1993 and is on display at the University of Vermont.

g3_ss.title: Vermont's Communities and Government
g3_ss.plan: Find Montpelier and Burlington, hold a class town meeting to vote on a question, and compare the jobs of the General Assembly (30 senators, 150 representatives), the Governor, and the Supreme Court.

g3_ss.title: Vermont's First Peoples
g3_ss.plan: Learn how the Abenaki lived in wigwams, farmed corn, beans, and squash, and made maple syrup, and meet the four state-recognized Abenaki tribes today.

g3_ss.title: Vermont Trailblazers
g3_ss.plan: Make trading cards for Gray Lock, Lucy Terry Prince, Lemuel Haynes, Alexander Twilight, Clarina Howard Nichols, Martin Henry Freeman, and Mary Annette Anderson, telling what first each one achieved or what each one stood up for.

g45_ss.title: Vermont's First Nations
g45_ss.plan: Trace 11,000 years of Native history in Ndakinna, from Paleo-Indian hunters to Abenaki farming villages, Gray Lock's resistance, the move to Odanak, and the fight for recognition.

g45_ss.title: From New France to the Vermont Republic, 1609–1791
g45_ss.plan: Follow Champlain (1609), Fort Sainte Anne (1666), the 1777 Republic and its first-in-the-nation constitution limiting slavery, the Battle of Bennington, and statehood in 1791.

g45_ss.title: Vermont, Freedom, and the Civil War, 1791–1877
g45_ss.plan: Study Windsor v. Jacob (1802), Alexander Twilight's firsts, Rokeby and the Underground Railroad, Frederick Douglass in Ferrisburgh, Vermont's Civil War soldiers, and the St. Albans Raid.

g3_sci.title: From Sap to Syrup
g3_sci.plan: Learn how sugar maples make sap, why Abenaki people boiled it into syrup, and why Vermont leads the nation in maple syrup.

g3_sci.title: Vermont Forest Animals
g3_sci.plan: Sort Vermont animals like deer, moose, beavers, bobcats, and hermit thrushes into forest and lake habitats and draw a food chain.

g3_sci.title: A Whale in Vermont?
g3_sci.plan: Use the Charlotte whale to learn how fossils form and how a beluga ended up buried far from the ocean.

g45_sci.title: Glaciers and the Champlain Sea
g45_sci.plan: Model how mile-thick ice pressed the land down, how the sea flooded in, and how the land rebounded, using the Charlotte whale as evidence.

g45_sci.title: Rocks of Vermont
g45_sci.plan: Compare granite, marble, and slate (state rocks) and talc (state mineral), and map where they are quarried.

g45_sci.title: Floods and a Changing Climate
g45_sci.plan: Compare the 1927 flood and Tropical Storm Irene (2011), graph Vermont's rising rainfall, and design ways towns can prepare.
